title: Architecting a Cloud Native Application
overview: Design services for elasticity, resilience, automation and observable operation. Start with state placement and the 12-factor practices, then connect immutable delivery, external configuration and orchestration. Use the design checklists to test scaling, availability, security, operations and feasibility against actual requirements.
big_ideas: Cloud native = Platforms (clouds, managed services) + Properties (scalable, loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, observable) + Practices (automation, CD, DevOps).
Treat servers as **cattle, not pets**: keep instances stateless and push state to shared or external stores so any instance can die without losing user data.

The 12-factor app (codebase, dependencies, config, backing services, build/release/run, processes, port binding, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs, admin processes) is the baseline recipe for cloud native services.
Config lives outside the artifact (environment variables), so the same immutable image runs in dev, test and prod.
Google's 5 principles: design for automation, be smart with state, favour managed services, practise defence in depth, always be architecting.
Cloud native vs traditional: speed over longevity, DevOps over silos, loosely coupled services over monoliths, horizontal on-demand scaling over vertical pre-provisioned scaling.
Maturity ladder: Cloud Ready, Cloud Friendly (12-factor), Cloud Resilient, Cloud Native (microservices, API-first).
Good design asks explicit questions on scalability, availability (SLAs are composite), security (data jurisdiction), manageability (monitoring, deployment) and feasibility (skills, cost, trade-offs).

sections.title: What is cloud native?
sections.summary: Defines cloud native architecture and applications, and introduces the three Ps (Platforms, Properties, Practices) and the wider map of ideas around cloud native.

notes.lead: Exploiting the cloud's very different constraints, not just hosting on it.
items: **Goal qualities**: scalable, portable, maintainable
**Capabilities**: resilient, scalable, observable, highly automated, easily updated
**Practices**: cooperation, integration and open governance between teams
**Platforms** → dynamic public, private or hybrid clouds and subscribed managed services
**Properties** → scalable, loosely coupled, resilient, manageable, observable, plus config and secrets
**Practices** → automation, continuous delivery, DevOps (frequent, predictable change)
**Resilience**: the ability to continue or recover after failure
**Elasticity / autoscaling**: adjusts capacity to demand
**Portability / open standards**: reduce some integration and switching costs
**Lock-in** still possible → provider-specific APIs and data dependencies
**Containers**
**Orchestration** (Kubernetes)
**Serverless**
**CNCF**: the foundation that curates this ecosystem
notes.foot: The goals they serve: **speed, resilience, scale and cost**.

terms.def: Building and running apps to exploit cloud platforms: resilient, scalable, observable, automated and easily updated.
Platforms, Properties and Practices that together characterise a cloud native application.
Applications automatically growing and shrinking to meet demand.
Cloud Native Computing Foundation, which hosts Kubernetes and related projects.

check.q: A company moved its app onto Kubernetes on a public cloud, but releases still happen quarterly by hand and nobody watches metrics. Is it cloud native? Use the three Ps.

items: **Properties** missing: **observable**, **resilient**, **loosely coupled**
**Practices** missing: **automation**, **continuous delivery**, **DevOps**
→ it gets little of the **speed**, **resilience** or **scale** that cloud native aims for
a.foot: Add **CI/CD**, **monitoring** and **automated recovery** before calling it cloud native.

check.q: A team says 'we use only open-standard containers, so we have no lock-in.' Do you agree?

items: **Open standards** → tools easier to **integrate**, can lower **switching costs**
**Lock-in also comes from provider-specific APIs**, **managed data services** and **operational dependencies**
**Check** each **managed service** the app uses, and how its **data would move**, before claiming **portability**

check.q: During a zone failure, an app's autoscaler added capacity but users still saw errors for 20 minutes. Which cloud-native property was missing, and why isn't autoscaling enough?

a.lead: **Resilience** was missing: the ability to **continue or recover after failure**.
items: **Autoscaling** adjusts **capacity to demand** only
It doesn't **reroute traffic** around a **failed zone** or replace **dependencies** that went down with it
**Resilience needs design work**: **multi-zone placement**, **health checks**, **failover**, **bounded retries**

sections.title: Service models, stack and principles
sections.summary: Compares IaaS, CaaS, PaaS, FaaS and SaaS by who manages what, contrasts the cloud native stack with a traditional web app, and covers Google's five principles and the container workflow.

notes.lead: Service models change the operating boundary.
items: **IaaS** → exposes VMs
**CaaS** → manages container-platform components
**PaaS** → manages the application runtime
**FaaS** → runs functions
**SaaS** → supplies a finished application
notes.foot: Exact duties vary by offering: **managed Kubernetes does not necessarily remove worker-node operations**, and **data accountability remains with the customer**.

items: **CaaS** → long-running or portable containerised workloads where you want runtime control
**FaaS** → short event-driven work where the platform handles runtime and autoscaling

notes.lead: Cloud native splits the traditional layered monolith.
items: **Cloud native** → pushes these into **independently deployable services**
**Security and observability** across the whole stack
**Design for automation**
**Be smart with state**
**Favour managed services**: spend effort on business code, not operations
**Practise defence in depth**
**Always be architecting**: design is continuous
**Write** the app
**Package** it as an image (app plus dependencies)
**Push** to a registry
**Pull**: a server pulls it
**Run**: the container runtime starts it
notes.foot: Gives **repeatable packaging on compatible platforms**; configuration and backing services still affect behaviour.

terms.def: Containers as a Service: a provider manages container-platform components; worker and workload duties depend on the offering.
Function as a Service (serverless): you deploy only functions; the platform handles runtime and autoscaling.
A packaged bundle of an app and its dependencies, stored in a registry.
Node software that pulls images and creates, starts, stops and deletes containers.

check.q: A new service processes uploaded documents within seconds of arrival, runs a few hundred times a day, and needs no special runtime. Another holds long-lived WebSocket connections. CaaS or FaaS for each?

items: **Document processor → FaaS**: **short, event-driven** work; the platform handles **runtime** and **autoscaling**; you **pay only when it runs**
**WebSocket service → CaaS**: **long-running** and needs **runtime control**, something **functions handle poorly**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: FaaS gives up **control** and **portability**; CaaS keeps them but **you operate more**.

check.q: A team chose managed Kubernetes and says they no longer have any infrastructure work. Is that right?

items: **CaaS** manages the **container platform components**
**Worker-node operations** such as **patching** and **scaling** may still fall to the **customer**, depending on the offering
**Data accountability** always stays with the customer
**Check** the provider's actual **responsibility split**
a.foot: '**Favour managed services**' moves effort to **business code** but doesn't remove all operations.

check.q: A container image passed every test in staging but fails in production with the same image tag. What is the most likely cause?

items: The **image fixes** the **app and dependency versions** only
**Behaviour also depends on** external **configuration**, **platform features** and **backing services** → these **differ between staging and production**
**Compare environment config**, **secrets**, **service endpoints** and **platform versions**
a.foot: Keeping **dev and prod sufficiently alike** reduces this.

visuals.title: Who manages what (slide 11)
visuals.caption: Simplified operating boundaries. Check the chosen service’s worker-node duties and shared data responsibilities.

sections.title: State: pets vs cattle
sections.summary: Explains why cloud native apps should be stateless, how sticky sessions differ from shared state, Kubernetes options for state, and VM-centric vs app-centric deployment.

notes.lead: Stateless instances do not own durable user state.
items: **Domain data** → store in databases
**Sessions** → shared store, or suitable client-held tokens
**Disposable caches** possible, but correctness must not depend on one instance's memory
notes.foot: Losing an instance should **not lose committed user data**.

notes.lead: An operating model, not a size or VM rule.
items: **Pet** → needs individual repair
**Cattle** → replaceable from automation
**Sticky routing** is fragile when session data exists only on that instance
**VMs can also be disposable**; **containers can still be operated as pets**
**StatefulSets** → stable ordering and identity
**Persistent Volumes and Claims** → cluster storage and requests for it
**Operators** → custom resources encoding operational knowledge
**External state stores** → databases or queues outside the cluster (e.g. managed cloud databases)
**In-cluster** → control and portability, but you operate it
**External managed store** → offloads backups, replication and patching; keeps the cluster stateless

terms.def: Application instance whose durable correctness does not depend on local domain or session state; persistent state is kept elsewhere.
Load balancer routes a user to the same instance every time, tying their session to that server.
Pets are hand-cared, irreplaceable servers; cattle are identical, disposable instances replaced automatically.
Kubernetes workload object giving stateful pods ordering and uniqueness guarantees.
Extension using custom resources to encode and automate operational knowledge for an application.

check.q: A web tier uses sticky sessions with session data held in instance memory. During a scale-in event, users are logged out. Diagnose it and fix it.

items: **Diagnosis**: **scale-in** removed instances that held the **only copy** of some sessions → **sticky routing** sent users to sessions that **no longer existed**
**Fix**: move **session state** to a **shared store**, or use suitable **client-held tokens** → any **ready instance** can serve the next request
a.foot: **Cost**: a shared store on the **request path** that must itself be **available**.

check.q: A team runs a database in Kubernetes with a StatefulSet. A reviewer suggests a managed external database instead. When is each right?

items: **External managed database** → usually the **better default**: the provider handles **backups**, **replication** and **patching**; the cluster stays **stateless**
**StatefulSet**, or an **Operator** that encodes **operational knowledge** → right when the store must **run in the cluster** for **control** or **portability**, and the team **accepts operating it**

check.q: A teammate says 'we're on containers, so our servers are cattle now.' What would show whether that is true?

a.lead: **Pets versus cattle** is an **operating model**, not a technology.
items: **Check**: can any instance be **deleted and recreated from automation** without **losing data** or needing someone to **fix it by hand**?
**Containers** that are **patched in place** or hold **unique local state** → still **pets**
**Disposable VMs** can be **cattle**

visuals.title: Any replica can serve the next request

steps.label: Client
steps.detail: The client reaches a stable entry point; it does not select a particular application instance.

steps.label: Load balancer
steps.detail: Requests can move between replicas during scaling, failure or rollout.

steps.label: Stateless replica
steps.detail: Process the request using shared backing services. Local caches must be disposable.

steps.label: External state
steps.detail: Keep domain and session data outside replaceable instances; design durability and availability for this store.

sections.title: The 12-factor app
sections.summary: The twelve practices that make a service suitable for cloud deployment.

items: **Codebase**: one tracked codebase, many deploys
**Dependencies**: declared and packaged
**Config**: in the environment
**Backing services**: attached resources via URL
**Build/release/run**: strictly separate stages
**Processes**: stateless
**Port binding**: self-contained service
**Concurrency**: scale out via processes
**Disposability**: fast start, graceful stop
**Dev/prod parity**
**Logs**: event streams
**Admin processes**: one-off tasks
**Build** → one immutable artifact
**Release** → artifact + environment-specific configuration
**Run** → execute that release
notes.foot: Promoting the **same tested artifact reduces drift**. A **rollback** also needs compatible configuration and data/schema state.

items: **Stateless shared-nothing processes** → hold no local state, so can be duplicated freely
**Scale-out concurrency** → add more processes
**Disposability** → fast startup and graceful shutdown let the platform add, remove and replace them at will
**Backing services are configured dependencies** → external addresses let deployments select compatible databases, queues or mail services **without rebuilding**
**Caveat**: a different protocol or data model can still require code changes
**Logs** → stream to central storage, because local files vanish with disposable instances
**Dev/prod parity** → keep dev and prod sufficiently alike to expose integration problems

terms.def: Methodology of twelve practices for building portable, scalable services suited to cloud platforms.
Any external resource (DB, queue, mail server) consumed over the network, attached via URL/config.
Processes keep no shared local state, so any can be added or removed freely.
Keeping all environments as similar as possible to avoid late surprises.

check.q: A team rebuilds the image separately for test and for production with different config baked in. Which factors does this break, and what is the risk?

a.lead: Breaks **build/release/run separation** and **config in the environment**.
items: **Risk**: the **production artifact** is not the one that was **tested** → builds can **drift** through **dependency or build differences**
**Fix**: build **one immutable artifact**, combine it with **environment config at release**, and **promote the same artifact**
a.foot: A **rollback** still needs **compatible config** and **schema state**.

check.q: An autoscaler adds instances during a spike, but each takes 3 minutes to start and loses in-flight work when removed. Which factors are failing, and why do they matter together?

items: **Concurrency through scale-out** only works if the platform can **add and remove processes freely**
**Slow starts** → capacity arrives **after the spike**
**Abrupt stops** → **lose work**

sub: Handle **termination signals** to **finish or hand back work**

check.q: After an incident, engineers can't find the logs because the failed containers were already replaced. Which factor was ignored, and what is the fix?

items: Instances are **disposable** → **local log files vanish** with them
**Fix**: write logs to **stdout** as a **stream**; the platform **ships** them to a **central aggregator** that can be **searched across all instances**
a.foot: **Cost**: running or paying for the **log pipeline** and its **storage**.

visuals.title: Build once, configure each release

steps.label: Code and dependencies
steps.detail: Track the application codebase and declare dependencies so the build is repeatable.

steps.label: Build artifact
steps.detail: Promote the same tested artifact through environments rather than rebuilding per environment.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: Combine the artifact with environment-specific backing-service addresses and protected secrets.

steps.label: Run processes
steps.detail: Use stateless processes, fast startup and graceful shutdown; stream logs and run admin tasks separately.

visuals.caption: Dev/prod parity checks that the same release assumptions hold across environments.

sections.title: Packaging, config and orchestration
sections.summary: Follows an app from code to a Kubernetes pod, covering the Kubernetes control plane, externalised configuration, the service mesh and application packages.

notes.h: Code to cluster: chain of runtimes
items: **Built application** → language runtime
**Container image** → container runtime
**Pod** → Kubernetes cluster
notes.foot: **Orchestration**, unlike running a container on one machine, spreads workloads across a **cluster of nodes**.

items: **Manifest** states the desired state: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec
**Control plane** (scheduling, scaling, self-healing) **continuously reconciles** reality to it
**Worker nodes** run the pods

notes.lead: So one artifact serves several environments.
items: **Environment variables** or **mounted external configuration** → avoid baking deploy-specific values into the image
**Secrets** → source from protected storage with restricted access
**Caveat**: environment variables alone do not make a secret secure
**Both** have a control plane and a data plane
**API gateway** → fronts external clients
**Service mesh** → manages service-to-service traffic (routing, resilience, observability, security) **without changing service code**
**Application package** → language-specific: program, same-language libraries, config
**Container image** → bundles the runtime environment too

terms.def: Smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes; one or more containers scheduled together on a node.
Management layer that schedules, scales and heals workloads (Kubernetes) or configures proxies (service mesh).
Declarative file (apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec) describing the desired state of a Kubernetes object.
Pattern managing service-to-service communication: routing, resilience, observability, security.
Settings kept outside the artifact, typically as environment variables.

check.q: A team puts its database password in an environment variable and calls it 'secure because it's not in the code'. Do you agree?

items: **Externalising config is right** → **one artifact** serves several **environments**
**An environment variable alone doesn't protect a secret** → it can **leak** through **logs**, **dumps** or anyone with access to the **deployment spec**
**Fix**: source it from **protected secret storage** with **restricted access** and **inject it at runtime**

check.q: Someone deletes a pod by mistake and it comes back a few seconds later. Explain why, and say what this means for how you change production.

items: The manifest declares a **desired state** (e.g. **3 replicas**)
The **control plane** continuously **reconciles** the cluster to it → it **recreated the pod**
**Change production** by changing the **declared state**, not by **editing live resources** → **reconciliation will undo manual fixes**

check.q: A platform has 25 internal services with inconsistent retry and encryption behaviour, plus a public mobile API. Where do an API gateway and a service mesh each fit?

items: **API gateway** → the **entry point** for the mobile clients' **external traffic**: **routing**, **authentication**, **rate limits**
**Service mesh** → the 25 services' **internal traffic**: consistent **routing**, **resilience**, **observability** and **encryption** without changing **service code**
**Both** have a **control plane** and a **data plane**
a.foot: The mesh adds **operating cost**, which is justified here by the **inconsistency across 25 services**.

steps.label: Application codebase
steps.detail: Built as a Java application; runs on a Java runtime.

steps.label: Container image
steps.detail: App and its dependencies packaged in one image; runs on a container runtime.

steps.label: Registry
steps.detail: Image is uploaded and shared in a registry; a server downloads it and runs it as a container.

steps.label: Manifest
steps.detail: Kubernetes manifest: spec is the state you desire for the object.

steps.label: Kubernetes
steps.detail: Control plane provides orchestration, scheduling, scaling and self-healing; apps are deployed as Pods onto the nodes of a cluster.

sections.title: Maturity, traditional vs cloud native, summary
sections.summary: A cloud native maturity model, a microservice retail example, traditional vs cloud native comparison, key attributes and design axes.

items: **Cloud Ready** → no permanent disk access, self-contained, platform-managed ports and backing services
**Cloud Friendly** → 12-factor, horizontally scalable, uses platform HA
**Cloud Resilient** → fault tolerant, cloud-agnostic runtime, bundled metrics, proactive failure testing
**Cloud Native** → microservices, API-first
**Traditional** → long release cycles, server-centric capacity planning
**Cloud native** → frequent automated delivery, disposable horizontally scaled services
notes.foot: These are **tendencies, not rules**: monoliths and VMs can also use DevOps and autoscaling.

notes.h: What a cloud native app is like
items: **Predictable**
**OS-abstracted**
**Right-sized**
**Collaborative**
**Continuously delivered**
**Independent** (small services)
**Automatically scalable**
**Quick to recover**
notes.foot: Together: **microservices, loose coupling, resilience, agility, automation, self-healing and a DevOps culture**.

items: **Clients** call an **API gateway**
**Gateway** fronts small services: search, cart, checkout, payments
**Some services own their own databases**
**Integrates** with back-end systems

terms.def: Four levels: Cloud Ready, Cloud Friendly, Cloud Resilient, Cloud Native.
Single entry point that routes client requests to back-end microservices.
Designing the service's API contract first so services integrate through well-defined APIs.
Adding more instances rather than making one machine bigger (vertical scaling).

check.q: A legacy app has been containerised but still writes to local disk and uses sticky sessions. Where is it on the maturity model, and what is the next step?

items: **Cloud Ready requires**: **no permanent disk access** + a **self-contained app** using **platform-managed backing services**
**First**: move **files and sessions** to **backing services**
**Then**: adopt the **12 factors** and **horizontal scaling** → **Cloud Friendly**
a.foot: **Containerising alone** doesn't move it up the **ladder**.

check.q: An app is 12-factor and scales horizontally on platform HA, and a team wants to call it 'cloud native'. What would it still need?

items: **Cloud Resilient** adds: **fault tolerance**, a **cloud-agnostic runtime**, **bundled metrics**, **proactive failure testing**
**Cloud Native** adds: **microservices** and **API-first design**
a.foot: Whether to **go further** depends on whether the business needs **independent deployability** and **resilience** that **justify the cost**.

check.q: A company adopted containers and microservices but kept separate dev and ops teams with handoffs, and releases are still slow. Why?

items: **Short continuous delivery** and **fast recovery** need **collaborating teams** and **automation** as well as the **technical properties**
**Handoffs between silos** → keep the **release cycle long**, whatever the **architecture**
**Fix**: pair the architecture with **DevOps practices** and **shared ownership**

steps.label: Cloud Ready
steps.detail: No permanent disk access; self-contained application; platform-managed ports and networking; consumes platform-managed backing services.

steps.label: Cloud Friendly
steps.detail: 12 Factor App methodology; horizontally scalable; leverages platform for high availability.

steps.label: Cloud Resilient
steps.detail: Fault-tolerant and resilient design; cloud-agnostic runtime; bundled metrics and monitoring; proactive failure testing.

sections.title: Design space, characteristics and guidelines
sections.summary: Levels of design abstraction, the characteristics to weigh when choosing a cloud, and guidelines for separation of concerns.

notes.lead: Start with the goal (productivity, ease of migration, or control), then weigh:
items: **Integration**
**Data storage and location**
**Ecosystem and portfolio**
**Pricing model**: fixed vs use-based
**QoS**: availability, DR, SLA
**Security and privacy**
**Self-service**
**Elasticity**
**Vendor viability**
**Migration** favours → backward compatibility, internal-network integration, data location
**New product** favours → productivity, elasticity, use-based pricing, rich managed-service portfolio
**Independent of** frameworks, UI, database and external agencies
**Testable without them**
**Organise code around the business problem**, not generic folders

notes.lead: Design thinking spans levels of abstraction:
items: **Technologies and mechanisms**
**Idioms and patterns**
**Architecture**

terms.def: Keeping business rules isolated from UI, database, frameworks and external systems so each can change independently.
The provider's commitment to cloud and ability to execute as a business.

check.q: Business rules for loan approval call the database driver and the web framework directly. The team now wants to change databases and unit-test the rules. What is the problem, and what would you change?

items: **Problem**: the rules are **coupled** to the **database and framework** → changing either means **rewriting logic**, and tests need a **real database**
**Separate concerns**: put the rules in code **independent of frameworks, UI, database and external agencies**
Reach the database through an **interface**

check.q: Two projects are choosing a cloud: migrating a legacy enterprise app with on-premises integrations, and building a new consumer product. Which characteristics should weigh most for each?

items: **Legacy migration** → weigh most: **ease of migration**, **backward compatibility**, **integration with the internal network**, **data location**
**New product** → weigh most: **productivity**, **elasticity**, **use-based pricing**, a rich **managed-service portfolio**
a.foot: The **same provider** can **win for one project and lose for the other** → start from each **project's goal**.

sections.title: Design considerations: scalability to feasibility
sections.summary: Checklists of questions an architect should answer on scalability, availability, security, manageability and feasibility.

items: **Ask**: which layers must scale, how fast, can you scale down off-hours?
**Persistence**: check limits and partition data
**Many small instances** over few large ones
**Dependencies**: identify those required for each request
**Series estimate**: for independent services in series, multiply availability probabilities; common failures and redundancy change the result
**Design**: failover, replication, bounded retries, circuit breakers
**Backups** protect against corruption as well as outages
**Test** restoration and idempotent replay
**Data residency**: where data legally resides, including failover and metrics copies
**Federated identity**
**Secured hybrid links**
**Access control** for admin portal and database
**Credential rotation**
**Multitenancy effects**
**Patching**
**Monitor** with usable, compliant storage of metrics and logs
**Auditing vs logging**: distinguish them
**Adjust levels at runtime**
**Deployment**: automated, verifiable, reversible, non-disruptive
**Environments**: a deliberate number of them
**SLAs**: can any provider meet them?
**Skills, budget and time**: do you have them?
**Operating costs**: what are they?
**Trade-offs**: what can be reduced (scope, SLAs, resilience) as an accepted trade-off

terms.def: End-to-end availability depends on the dependency structure; independent required services in series have multiplied availability probabilities.
Multiple consumers read from one queue so work is spread and load is levelled.
Pattern that stops calling a failing service for a while to avoid cascading failure and overload.
An operation that can be repeated (e.g. a replayed message) without changing the result beyond the first time.

check.q: A checkout request needs an API service, a payment service and a database in series, each at 99.9% availability. A manager promises 99.9% end-to-end. Is that realistic?

items: **0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%** → the path is **less available than any single part**
**An estimate**: **shared failure modes** and **redundancy** change it
a.foot: **To reach 99.9%**: add **redundancy** or **failover** on the **critical path**, or **reduce dependencies** the request needs.

check.q: Order submissions spike tenfold at sale start, and the order processor falls over. How do queues help, and what must the consumers guarantee?

items: **Queue** between submission and processing → **producers aren't blocked**
**Backlog levels the peak**
**Competing consumers** scale out to **drain it**
**Consumer fails** → the message is **delivered again** → processing must be **idempotent** to avoid **duplicate orders**
a.foot: **Trade-off**: users now get '**accepted**' rather than '**completed**' immediately.

check.q: The primary database is replicated to a second region, so the team drops nightly backups. What risk does this create?

items: **Replication copies** an **accidental delete** or a **corrupting update** to **every replica** → nothing earlier to recover
**Backups** keep **recoverable earlier states**
**Keep backups**, **test restores** against acceptable **data loss** and **recovery time**, and make **replay idempotent**

check.q: Customer data must stay in Singapore. The app's database is in Singapore, but failover is to another country's region and metrics go to a global monitoring service. Is the design compliant?

items: **Data protection rules apply to every copy**, including **failover replicas** and any **customer data inside metrics or logs**
**Failover**: choose an **in-country** location, or **confirm the rules allow** it
**Telemetry**: **scrub personal data**, or keep it **in-region**

exam_angles.q: A retailer's monolithic web shop loses customers' carts whenever a server crashes and can't cope with sale-day spikes of 20 times normal traffic. Diagnose the causes and propose a cloud native redesign, naming one new risk it introduces.

sub: The **single scaling unit** can't **grow fast enough**
**Stateless web tier**, with carts in a **shared store** or **managed database**
Split **hot areas** such as **checkout** into **services** behind an **API gateway**
Put **order processing behind a queue** → **level peaks**

exam_angles.q: Audit this service against the 12 factors: config is baked into images per environment, logs go to local files, the service takes 4 minutes to start, it writes uploads to local disk, and a database migration runs at every container start. Rank the gaps by operational risk and give the fix for each.

sub: Breaks **stateless processes** → **data is lost** when instances are **replaced**
Breaks **build/release/run** and **config** → the **tested artifact** isn't the one **deployed**
**Fix**: **build once** and **inject config at release**, with **secrets** from **protected storage**

exam_angles.q: You must offer 99.95% availability for a service whose request path uses a gateway, a compute tier and a managed database, each with a 99.9% SLA. Explain why the target is at risk and propose design changes, with the cost of each.

sub: **Provider SLAs alone** can't guarantee the **end-to-end figure**
Possibly a **second region** for the **most critical path**

items: **Remove dependencies** from the **synchronous path** using **queues** and **caches**
**Bound retries** and use **circuit breakers** → one **slow dependency** doesn't **cascade**
a.foot: **Cost**: each step adds **cost and complexity** → check **feasibility**; if the **budget or skills** can't support it, **renegotiate the SLA**.

exam_angles.q: A bank's 20-year-old core app is released twice a year, runs on large VMs sized for peak, and is owned by separate dev and ops teams. A new digital-banking team wants weekly releases. Contrast the traditional and cloud-native approaches for each part, and say whether the core app should be converted.

items: **Digital team** → should **build cloud native**

items.t: **Core app**: doesn't need to **convert all at once**
sub: **Expose it through APIs** and **modernise** where **business drivers** justify it
These are **tendencies** → the core app can adopt **automation** and **DevOps without a rewrite**

exam_angles.q: You run 30 microservices on Kubernetes across dev, test and prod. Secrets are in plain manifests, retries differ per team, and an outage last month cascaded through internal calls. Propose how to manage configuration, secrets and service-to-service traffic.

items: **Ordinary config** → **outside the image**, **per environment** → the **same artifact** is **promoted** through all three
**Secrets** → **protected secret storage** with **restricted access**, **injected at runtime** → **plain manifests** or **environment variables** alone aren't protection
**Declare everything** in **version-controlled manifests** → the **control plane reconciles drift**

items.t: **Service-to-service traffic** → a **service mesh**, justified by **30 services** and a **cascading outage**
sub: Consistent **timeouts**, **bounded retries**, **circuit breaking**, **encryption** and **tracing without code changes**

a.foot: The mesh adds **operational overhead** and **latency** to manage.
